name: Amiloxate

lead: Amiloxate is a cinnamate-type UVB filter found in some sunscreens. People use sunscreens with filters like it to prevent sunburn and the cumulative photoaging that shows up as uneven tone and wrinkles.

It absorbs UVB radiation within the sunscreen film. Published work on it is mostly analytical and environmental, plus case reports of photoallergic contact dermatitis; its appearance benefit follows from the general effect of sunscreens.

paras: It is an ingredient in EU sunscreens, usually combined with other filters in a daily or holiday SPF. Benefits come from regular application over months and years rather than from a visible change after one use.
Photoallergic contact dermatitis has been reported. It is not an approved US OTC sunscreen active.

angle.text: Amiloxate is a cinnamate UVB filter found in EU sunscreens. By absorbing UVB it lowers sunburn, and over time less sun damage means skin stays more even and youthful. Published work on it consists mainly of analytical studies and photoallergy case reports.

lead: Amiloxate (isoamyl p-methoxycinnamate, isopentyl 4-methoxycinnamate, IMC) is a cinnamate ester used as a UVB filter in sunscreen products [1]. It has been approved in the European Union since 1997; in the United States it has been under regulatory evaluation rather than listed as an approved sunscreen active [1].
Published literature on it consists mainly of analytical methods, environmental occurrence studies, and photoallergy reports.
infobox: Under evaluation (not an approved OTC active)

paras: Amiloxate appears among the UV filters measured in commercial suncare formulations and cosmetics by chromatography methods [2][3][4]. In a mouse inflammation assay of the 21 UV filters then authorised in Europe, 13 showed anti-inflammatory effects; researchers proposed this might explain differences between in vivo and in vitro SPF measurements [5].

A 15-year review of sunscreen allergy found that 20% of 402 patients tested had allergic or photoallergic contact dermatitis to one or more UV absorbers [6]. A case report described photoallergic contact dermatitis due to isoamyl p-methoxycinnamate in a sunscreen marketed as organic [7], and another study reported photoallergy to UV filters across several sunscreens [8].

Amiloxate has been measured in indoor dust [9] and in a freshwater recreational reservoir, where researchers examined its dissipation [10]. Porcine-skin work found chemical UV absorbers largely remained in the outer stratum corneum in a barrier-mimetic formulation [11].

No clinical trials specific to amiloxate were found. It was among the filters evaluated in a registered multicentre European photopatch study (1,000 participants) [12], and in the allergy series described above [6].
